220: The weights above were assigned rather than computed, so the ranking was verified against a second set of weights derived from the data themselves. Principal component analysis was performed on the merit scores, and each attribute was then weighted by the sum, over the components with an eigenvalue of one or more, of its squared loading multiplied by the share of variance that component carries. This is the customary procedure for assigning weights to a composite indicator without recourse to judgement. The two rankings corresponded closely, with a mean Spearman correlation of 0.942 and a minimum of 0.867, and the same cultivar ranked first in 3 of the 4 products, as Table 30 demonstrates. The ranking therefore proceeds from the data and not from the particular weights adopted. Principal component analysis is employed here solely to assign the weights; the components themselves cannot rank the cultivars for quality, since a component measures the direction of greatest variation and takes no account of whether a high or a low value is the more desirable.
223: The mean rank correlation was 0.942 and the minimum 0.867, and the same cultivar ranked first in 3 of the 4 products. The ranking is therefore not an artefact of the weights adopted. Where the two diverged, the cultivars concerned were in any case closely positioned on the index, so that the divergence is one of order between near-equals rather than of substance.
226: Cluster analysis was employed to examine how the cultivars and the products group together when all the attributes are considered simultaneously. The 40 cultivar and product combinations were standardised on the 22 attributes determined in every product, and Ward's method was applied to the Euclidean distances between them, the number of groups being set at 4. Where a cluster contains only one product, the method of preparation determines the quality profile; where cultivars of different products fall together, the two are comparable in the finished form.
231: Of the 4 clusters, 3 contain only one product. This indicates that the products differ from one another to a greater extent than the cultivars differ within any one product. Amarnath and Ravi Kumar (2025) applied Ward's method comparably in rice and drew upon the cluster means to select genotypes for further work, on the reasoning that crosses between distant clusters are more likely to generate useful variation. Dutta and Mahanta (2014) advanced the same point from the product side, namely that different traditional preparations require genuinely different raw material.
234: Nine traditional aromatic rice cultivars of West Bengal were evaluated against Dudeshwar, a non-aromatic cultivar serving as the control, in the 4 cooked products of this group. Each was grown and prepared identically for two years and analysed as a pooled completely randomised design. In every product the cultivars differed significantly for nearly all the attributes determined, whereas year and its interaction with cultivar were significant for considerably fewer. The principal finding is therefore unambiguous: the choice of cultivar determines the quality of the product, and the year of production is of markedly less consequence. A cultivar selected on one year of results will generally retain its position in the next.
235: On this index the superior cultivar was Kalojira for table rice, Radhunipagal for kichidi, Kataribhog for pulao and Gobindabhog for payash. The control ranked at or near the bottom in every product, so that substituting the cultivars named here for Dudeshwar would improve the product without any alteration in the method of preparation. Table 28 gives, for each product, the cultivar exhibiting the best balance of attributes relative to the control.

237: Cluster analysis was then performed on all 40 cultivar and product combinations together, using the 22 attributes determined in every product. Ward's method resolved them into 4 groups, of which 3 contained a single product only (Table 31 and Fig. 27). When the products are compared with one another, therefore, it is the method of preparation rather than the cultivar that determines the broad quality type, whereas within any one product the cultivar is the variable under the processor's control. The two findings are complementary rather than contradictory: the preparation determines the type of product and the cultivar its standing within that type.
238: The cultivars identified here should be re-evaluated on a larger scale and over additional years before being recommended generally. For breeding work directed at improving the group as a whole, parents are best drawn from different clusters, since crosses between distant clusters are more likely to release useful variation.

249: Discussion. Amylose content determines the firmness and discreteness of the cooked grain: a higher content yields a firmer, drier grain that retains its shape, and a lower content a softer, stickier one. Amylose is deposited by granule-bound starch synthase I at the Waxy locus, and cultivars differ in the allele they carry. Cooking disorganises the granule but does not alter the quantity of amylose present.
250: Earlier work is largely concordant. Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) determined that apparent amylose governs eating and processing behaviour; Tian et al. (2018) that crystallinity and digestibility decline without any change in amylose; Cheng et al. (2019) that heat and moisture reconstitute the matrix into a firmer gel; and Devi and Badwaik (2022) that amylose accounts for most of the varietal difference in cooking behaviour. The most favourable entry varied between products, Kalojira and Kalonunia each ranking highest in one product or another, so that selection is contingent upon the product concerned.

254: The cultivars differed significantly in every product. Neither year nor its interaction with cultivar was significant, so that the order held in both years. Coefficients of variation ranged from 0.31 to 1.41 %, indicating good experimental precision.
256: Discussion. Starch constitutes the energy-supplying fraction of the grain and the basis of its texture; a higher value indicates a well-filled endosperm and good recovery of the edible fraction. Starch content is contingent upon the efficiency with which assimilate was translocated into the endosperm during grain filling, and in the prepared product it is further modified by the loss of low-molecular-weight material and by the water imbibed during cooking.
257: This is consistent with previous studies. Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) determined that starch constitutes approximately nine tenths of milled rice on a dry weight basis; Tian et al. (2018) that the residual starch is swollen and less crystalline; Iqbal et al. (2021) that restructured starch resists digestion; and Cheng et al. (2019) that the extent of starch gelatinisation governs texture and digestibility. Harinakhuri returned the most favourable value in every product of this group and is therefore the cultivar to select where a high value is required.

261: The cultivar effect was significant throughout the group. Neither year nor its interaction with cultivar was significant, so that the order held in both years. Coefficients of variation ranged from 2.46 to 4.36 %, indicating good experimental precision.
263: Discussion. Protein constitutes the principal nutritional contribution of rice after energy and additionally firms the cooked grain through disulphide bonding. The greater part of the protein is glutelin sequestered in protein bodies beneath the aleurone, and the quantity is contingent upon the nitrogen translocated into the grain during filling. Cooking does not alter it.
264: Published work is concordant. Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) determined that total protein is unaltered by hydrothermal treatment; Cheng et al. (2019) that disulphide cross-links elevate firmness; Akter et al. (2025) that protein rose from 6.68 to 9.42 per cent following treatment; and Iqbal et al. (2021) that the protein network governs enzyme access to starch. The leading position was shared between Gobindabhog, Kalojira and Radhunipagal, so that selection on this attribute must be made product by product.

270: Discussion. Soluble protein is the fraction remaining extractable, and therefore digestible, after cooking; a higher value indicates that heat has not aggregated the protein. Heat ruptures the protein bodies and subsequently cross-links the liberated chains through disulphide bonds, thereby reducing the extractable fraction, and cultivars richer in cysteine forfeit more.
271: The same pattern has been reported previously. Muchlisyiyah et al. (2023) determined that solubility alters while total protein does not; Cheng et al. (2019) that cross-linking reduces the extractable fraction; Kabir et al. (2025) that treatment modifies the association between protein and bound phenolics; and Roy et al. (2019) that solubility declines as steaming and soaking become more severe. Kalojira, Kataribhog and Radhunipagal each headed the ranking in a different product, so that this attribute cannot determine the selection for the group as a whole.
